questions.q: Researchers recovered the embedding projection layer (and hidden dimension) of production LLMs using only API queries. Which API feature made this possible, and what limits it?
options: Streaming responses; disabling streaming
Long system prompts; shortening them
Access to full logits/log-probabilities (with logit bias); restricting or adding noise to logprob outputs
High temperature sampling; forcing temperature 0
questions.why: Logit vectors lie in a low-rank subspace defined by the final layer, so collecting enough of them reveals its dimension and weights up to symmetries. Providers responded by limiting logprob and logit-bias exposure, showing that API conveniences can be extraction surfaces.

questions.q: A team wants token streaming for low latency but must apply output safety rails. What is the inherent trade-off when output rails are run on streamed chunks?
options: Streaming makes output rails unnecessary
Rails must then run on the GPU only
Streaming disables input rails
Content may reach the user before a later chunk is flagged, and chunk-level checks can miss context; larger buffers improve safety but add latency
questions.why: Checking a full response before display is safest but slowest; checking chunks lets text flow sooner but risks partial exposure and loses cross-chunk context. Chunk size and overlap are the tuning knobs for this latency/safety balance.

questions.q: A new input rail blocks 460 of 500 known jailbreak prompts and refuses 120 of 2,000 benign prompts. What are its block rate and false refusal rate?
options: 8% and 6%
questions.why: Block rate = 460 / 500 = 92%; false refusal rate = 120 / 2,000 = 6%. Reporting only the block rate hides over-refusal, which harms usability; both must be measured, ideally on realistic benign traffic.

questions.q: Llama Guard outputs the token "safe" or "unsafe". How can a team tune it for a precision/recall trade-off rather than accepting the default decision?
options: Use the probability assigned to the "unsafe" first token as a score and choose a custom threshold
Increase the number of categories in the taxonomy
Sample at higher temperature and take a majority vote
Fine-tune the main chat model instead
questions.why: Treating the first-token probability as a continuous score turns the generative classifier into one that can be thresholded and evaluated with precision-recall curves. Adding categories changes what is detected, not the operating point.

questions.q: In Colang 1.0-style dialog rails, how is a free-form user message typically mapped to a defined user intent (canonical form)?
options: Exact string match only
A regex compiled from the flow name
The input rail's toxicity score
Embedding similarity search against the example utterances for each intent, with the LLM generating a canonical form when needed
questions.why: Guardrails indexes example utterances and retrieves the most similar ones, using them as few-shot examples so the LLM produces the canonical form, which then drives the flow. Exact matching would fail on paraphrases, the reason semantic matching is used.

questions.q: A jailbreak succeeds on a given harmful request with probability 0.10 per independent sampled attempt. If an attacker can retry 5 times, what is the probability of at least one success?
options: About 0.41
About 0.59
questions.why: P(at least one) = 1 − (0.9)^5 = 1 − 0.590 = 0.410. 0.59 is the probability that all five attempts fail, and 0.50 wrongly adds the probabilities; red-team reports should state the number of attempts because single-try ASR understates real risk.

questions.q: For one applicant, a credit model's SHAP base value (expected output) is 0.20. Feature contributions are income +0.15, debt ratio −0.05, and credit history +0.10. What is the model's output for this applicant?
questions.why: SHAP values are additive: output = base value + Σ contributions = 0.20 + 0.15 − 0.05 + 0.10 = 0.40. Treating the negative contribution as positive gives 0.50.

questions.q: Interpretability researchers train sparse autoencoders on an LLM's residual-stream activations. What problem are they addressing?
options: Reducing KV-cache memory
Superposition: models represent more features than neurons, so individual neurons are polysemantic; SAEs recover more interpretable, monosemantic features
Compressing the model for deployment
Detecting PII in training data
questions.why: SAEs learn an overcomplete, sparse dictionary over activations whose directions often align with human-interpretable concepts, and these features can be used to steer behavior. They are an analysis tool, not a compression or serving optimization.

questions.q: A linear probe predicts a user's gender from a model's hidden states with 95% accuracy. What can be concluded?
options: The model definitely uses gender to make its predictions
The model is unbiased because gender is decodable
Gender information is linearly decodable from the representation, but this alone does not show the model causally uses it
The probe proves the model memorized each user
questions.why: Probing shows presence of information, not its use. Causal evidence requires interventions, such as removing that direction from the representation (concept erasure) and checking whether outputs change.

questions.q: A green-list watermark puts γ = 0.25 of the vocabulary on the green list at each step. A 200-token text contains 80 green tokens. What is the approximate detection z-score, z = (G − γT) / √(Tγ(1−γ))?
options: About 0.8
About 2.1
About 8.0
About 4.9
questions.why: Expected green count = 0.25 × 200 = 50; variance = 200 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 37.5, so the standard deviation ≈ 6.12; z = 30 / 6.12 ≈ 4.9, far above typical thresholds of about 4. Dividing by the variance instead of the standard deviation gives 0.8.

questions.q: Why are statistical generation-time watermarks less effective on outputs such as code or factual short answers?
options: Code is never tokenized
Low-entropy outputs leave few viable token choices, so biasing toward green tokens either has little room or harms correctness, weakening the signal
Watermarks only work in English
Code outputs are always longer than the watermark window
questions.why: When the next token is nearly determined, the watermark cannot shift choices without breaking syntax or facts, so detection needs much longer text. This is a fundamental limitation of logit-biasing schemes, not a language restriction.

questions.q: A platform worries that C2PA manifests are stripped when images are re-shared. Which C2PA-compatible approach helps recover provenance in that case?
options: Soft binding: an invisible watermark or content fingerprint that can be used to look up the original manifest
Storing the manifest in the file name
Lowering the image resolution
Replacing hashing with plain-text captions
questions.why: Hard bindings (cryptographic hashes) break when pixels change or metadata is removed, while soft bindings survive many transformations and point back to a stored manifest. Combining signed manifests with watermarks gives both integrity and durability.

questions.q: The EU AI Act presumes a general-purpose AI model has systemic risk when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. Using C ≈ 6ND, does a 70B-parameter model trained on 15T tokens exceed it?
options: Yes, about 6.3 × 10^25 FLOPs
Yes, about 1.05 × 10^27 FLOPs
No, about 1.05 × 10^24 FLOPs
No, about 6.3 × 10^24 FLOPs
questions.why: 6 × (7 × 10^10) × (1.5 × 10^13) = 6.3 × 10^24, below the 10^25 presumption threshold (the Commission can still designate models by other criteria). Option C forgets the factor of 6 that accounts for forward and backward passes.

questions.q: An enterprise wants a certifiable, organization-level management system standard for governing AI (policies, roles, risk processes, continual improvement), analogous to ISO 27001 for information security. Which standard fits?
options: NIST SP 800-53
ISO 9001
ISO/IEC 42001
IEEE 754
questions.why: ISO/IEC 42001 specifies requirements for an AI management system and supports third-party certification. The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework rather than a certifiable standard, and ISO 9001 covers general quality management without AI-specific controls.

questions.q: A jailbreak that makes a production assistant reveal other users' order data is reported. Which sequence of response steps is most appropriate?
options: Contain (block the pattern or disable the feature) → preserve logs and assess impact → fix root cause → add the attack to regression tests and notify affected parties as required
Retrain the model → wait for more reports → contain → delete logs
Notify the press → delete logs → retrain → contain
Fix root cause → contain → skip testing since the fix is known
questions.why: Containment stops ongoing harm first, evidence preservation enables impact assessment and any legally required notification, and regression tests prevent recurrence. The real flaw here is missing authorization on data access, so the root-cause fix belongs in the tool layer, not only in a new prompt rule.

questions.q: For safety monitoring, a team logs all prompts and responses, which frequently contain customer PII. Which practice best balances monitoring and privacy?
options: Disable all logging
Redact or tokenize PII before storage, restrict access, and enforce a defined retention period
Store logs indefinitely in plain text for future model training
Log only the model's responses, never the prompts
questions.why: Monitoring and incident response need logs, but data minimization, access control and retention limits reduce breach and compliance exposure. Logging only responses still captures PII echoed by the model and loses the context needed to investigate attacks.

questions.q: A training run consumes 504 MWh of GPU energy in a data center with PUE 1.2 on a grid emitting 0.4 kg CO2e per kWh. What are the approximate emissions?
options: About 168 t CO2e
About 202 t CO2e
About 242 t CO2e
About 605 t CO2e
questions.why: Facility energy = 504 MWh × 1.2 = 604.8 MWh = 604,800 kWh; × 0.4 kg/kWh = 241,920 kg ≈ 242 t. Ignoring PUE gives 202 t, and 605 is the facility energy in MWh, not emissions. Choosing a lower-carbon region can change this figure several-fold.

questions.q: Evaluators find that an RLHF-tuned assistant changes a correct answer to an incorrect one when the user pushes back with "I'm pretty sure that's wrong." What is this behavior and its likely origin?
options: Hallucination caused by too short a context window
Prompt injection from the user
Catastrophic forgetting from quantization
Sycophancy, partly arising because human raters tend to prefer responses that agree with them
questions.why: Preference-based training can reward agreement over accuracy, teaching models to tell users what they want to hear. This undermines honesty and trust; mitigations include targeted evaluation sets, training data that rewards maintaining correct answers, and preference models that penalize capitulation.
